findings.title: Denial cache is never invalidated and can re-deny newly granted (e.g. newly created) resources for 30s
findings.body: The new permission-denial cache is written whenever a full DB re-query returns not-allowed (service.go:154) and is consulted at the top of Check (service.go:117) to short-circuit to `Allowed:false` without any re-validation. No code path ever deletes these keys on permission changes; they only expire via `shortCacheTTL` (30s). Consequence: once a check is denied, a subsequent grant (including the exact "creator of a just-created dashboard/folder" scenario this PR targets, e.g. a check that runs before the grant is committed) keeps returning `Allowed:false` for up to 30s, reintroducing the bug the PR is meant to fix. Also, because the cache hit is decided by key presence rather than the stored value, any future code that stores `false` under this key would still deny. Consider invalidating denial keys on permission writes (or making this cache consistent with the freshness guarantee of the allow path).

findings.title: Every denied check now performs a full DB permission query
findings.body: When the cached permission map is present but does not contain the requested resource, `checkPermission` returns false and Check falls through to `s.getIdentityPermissions` (service.go:139). Since the cache read inside `getUserPermissions` was removed, this path always executes a full DB query (user identifiers, basic role, teams, permissions). The only thing that prevents a DB query on a repeat denied check is the per-resource denial cache. Consequence: the first check for each distinct resource a user cannot access now hits the DB, whereas previously the cached permission map short-circuited it. For denial-heavy traffic or checks over many inaccessible resources, this is a substantial increase in DB load. Consider recording that a cached permission set is known-complete/current so genuine denials can be served without a DB round-trip.

findings.title: Ambiguous denial-cache key can collide across distinct resources
findings.body: `userPermDenialCacheKey` joins namespace, user, action, name and parent with '_' without escaping, so different tuples can produce the same key. For example (action="a", name="b_c", parent="d") and (action="a_b", name="c", parent="d") both produce `...perm_<uid>_a_b_c_d`. Folder/dashboard UIDs and parent UIDs can contain underscores, so two distinct resources can map to the same denial key. Consequence: a denial cached for one resource is then served for a different resource the user may be allowed to access (up to the TTL). Use an unescapable delimiter or length-prefix/hash the components.

findings.title: List has no DB fallback for a stale permission map, so newly created resources are omitted
findings.body: `List` only re-queries the DB when `getCachedIdentityPermissions` returns an error, i.e. when the entire per-action permission map is absent. When the map is present but stale, `List` builds its response purely from that cached map, so scopes for dashboards/folders created after the map was cached are omitted for up to `shortCacheTTL` (30s). If the reported issue is observed through listing (new resource not appearing right after creation), this path remains unfixed: only `Check` received the DB fallback on a cache miss. Consider applying the same freshness handling to `List`.
